findings.title: parseDiff treats an added content line beginning with '++ ' as a new file header
findings.property: an added line inside a hunk never changes the current file; changed ranges stay attributed to the right file
findings.actual: '+++ x' (an added line with content '++ x') is parsed as a file header: file becomes 'x', a bogus entry 'x' is created and the later hunk is attributed to it, so a.txt loses range [11,11]
findings.evidence: parseDiff is documented to parse git diff --unified=0 into file -> new-side ranges; with unified=0 added lines are printed as '+' + content, so content '++ x' yields '+++ x' inside a hunk. The parser does not track hunk line counts, so it cannot tell it from a header. Changed functions in the real file can be missed in diff mode.

review.title: parseDiff treats an added line whose content starts with '++ ' as a new file header
review.reason: parseDiff checks `^\+\+\+ ` on every line and never tracks hunk line counts or the preceding `---` line. A real `git diff --unified=0` prints an added line with content `++ x` as `+++ x` inside a hunk. The parser then switches `file` to 'x', creates a bogus entry, and attributes all later hunks to it, so the real file loses ranges. The input is valid git output, and the expected result follows from the function's documented purpose of mapping each file to its new-side ranges. Diff mode could then skip changed functions, and a maintainer would accept a fix that consumes hunk bodies by count or only accepts `+++` right after a `---` line.

fix.reason: the repro passes on the patched code

findings.title: parseJavaTrace attributes frames of tab-indented 'Suppressed:' exceptions to the main exception
findings.property: frames of a suppressed exception are not included in the frames of the primary exception
findings.property_test: suppressed frames are not attributed to the main exception
findings.input:
java.lang.RuntimeException: boom
	at p.A.run(A.java:3)
	Suppressed: java.io.IOException: x
		at p.B.close(B.java:9)
findings.expected: frames only for A.java (the code splits the trace at Caused by/Suppressed to keep only the primary exception)
findings.actual: frames contains both A.java and B.java, because the split regex /\n(?:Caused by|Suppressed): / requires the keyword at column 0
findings.evidence: Java's Throwable.printStackTrace emits suppressed exceptions as '\tSuppressed: ...' (tab-indented); the code's own split on 'Suppressed: ' shows it intends to cut them off.

error.message:
Expected values to be strictly deep-equal:
+ actual - expected

  [
+   '/p/B.java',
    '/p/A.java'
  ]

review.title: parseJavaTrace does not cut off tab-indented 'Suppressed:' sections, so their frames are attributed to the primary exception
review.reason: src/lang/java.js:217 splits on /\n(?:Caused by|Suppressed): / to keep only the primary exception. Throwable.printStackTrace indents suppressed exceptions with a tab ('\tSuppressed: ...'), and a cause nested inside a suppressed exception is also indented. So the Suppressed branch of the regex can never match real JVM output, and the frame regex (/^\s*at .../gm) then collects the suppressed exception's frames. The repro is valid, and the intent is clear from the code. Changing the split to /\n\s*(?:Caused by|Suppressed): / is a small, safe fix that a maintainer would accept. Impact is limited to traces that contain suppressed exceptions.

findings.title: extractJSON returns inner object instead of enclosing array when wrapped in prose
findings.property: a JSON value embedded in prose is extracted intact
findings.actual: {a:1} (the first object; '{' is searched before '[' regardless of position)
findings.evidence: Docstring: 'Find the first JSON object/array in text'. The array starts before the object, so it is first; an array of objects is a common agent output.

review.title: extractJSON prefers '{' over '[' regardless of position, so an array of objects in prose returns its first element
review.reason: The docstring promises the first JSON object/array in the text. The loop in src/util.js:130 tries '{' before '[' without comparing positions. For `Result: [{"a":1},{"b":2}]`, whole-text parsing fails, the '{' pass then parses the first inner object, and the enclosing array is silently truncated. The existing tests don't catch this: the fenced array case succeeds through the direct JSON.parse of the fence contents, and the prose case only uses an object. A fix is trivial (try whichever opener comes first, falling back to the other), so a maintainer would accept it. Impact is limited because the current callers mostly expect objects.

findings.property_test: fmtMs never prints 60s or NNmSS with SS>=60
findings.evidence: Time formats NmSS must have seconds in 00-59; Math.round(s % 60) and toFixed(0) can reach 60 without carrying.

review.title: fmtMs rounds seconds up to 60 without carrying (e.g. '1m60s', '60s')
review.reason: In src/util.js, `fmtMs(119500)` floors minutes to 1 and then applies `Math.round(59.5)` to the seconds, which gives '1m60s' instead of '2m00s'. For `fmtMs(59600)`, `(59.6).toFixed(0)` gives '60s' instead of '1m00s'. The function formats durations as NmSS, where seconds are 00-59, so these outputs are invalid. The repro uses the function correctly and involves no float artefact. The fix is small: round the total to whole seconds before splitting into minutes and seconds. This is cosmetic, since it only affects log and report timing strings.

findings.property_test: relPath of child inside root is relative

review.title: relPath returns the absolute path for children whose name starts with '..'
review.reason: `relPath` in src/util.js:144 uses `r.startsWith('..')` to detect paths outside the root. `path.relative('/root', '/root/..foo/a.js')` returns `'..foo/a.js'`, which is inside the root, so `relPath` wrongly falls back to the absolute path. Valid names like `..foo` or `...` are rare, but a maintainer would accept the one-line fix of checking `r === '..' || r.startsWith('..' + path.sep)`. I did not run the repro myself; I confirmed the cause by reading the source.

findings.title: parseGoJson blames a package-level panic on every already-failed test, not just the one that died
findings.property: a test that finished with an explicit fail event keeps its own assertion error even if a different test later panics in package output
findings.property_test: a test that failed on its own does not inherit another test's panic
findings.input: TestA: output '    a_test.go:3: got 1, want 2' then fail; TestB: run only; package-level output 'panic: boom'
findings.expected: TestA error = AssertionError 'got 1, want 2' (only the unfinished TestB may take the panic)
findings.actual: TestA error is re-parsed from its lines plus the package output and becomes type 'panic', message 'boom'
findings.evidence: The comment says 'a panic printed after the test's own lines lands in package output', i.e. it is meant for the test that was running; but the condition only checks outcome === 'failed' and that the test's own lines lack 'panic:', so every failed test with a t.Error is overwritten.

error.message:
Expected values to be strictly equal:
+ actual - expected

+ 'panic'
- 'AssertionError'

review.title: parseGoJson attributes a package-level panic to every earlier failed test, not just the unfinished one
review.reason: The override at go.js:154 only checks that outcome is 'failed', that the test's own lines lack 'panic:', and that package output contains 'panic:'. It never checks whether the test finished. In `go test -json`, tests run sequentially, so a test that already got an explicit `fail` event has finished and cannot have caused a later panic. Its genuine t.Error message is replaced with type 'panic' and the other test's message. The code comment says the panic belongs to the test that was running, which is only the test with no outcome (the one set to 'failed' at line 147). Restricting the override to tests that had no explicit fail/pass event is a small fix a maintainer would accept. The repro matches the code path.

fix.reason: the repro passes on the patched code
